title: Centre Tells Supreme Court It Will Not Pursue FIRs Against Peaceful Student Protesters
excerpt: The Indian government has reaffirmed its commitment to the Supreme Court that it will not pursue criminal cases against students who protested peacefully over the NEET exam paper leak scandal.
body:
• The Centre has told the Supreme Court it is serious about its commitment to not pursue FIRs against peaceful student protesters arrested during the NEET exam leak agitation.
  • The Supreme Court has ordered no coercive action against protesters without criminal backgrounds and directed the immediate release of all detained minors.
  • Protest leaders accuse the government of backtracking on earlier assurances to fully withdraw FIRs, threatening fresh nationwide agitation if cases are not dropped.

The Indian government has told the Supreme Court it remains serious about its commitment to not pursue First Information Reports (FIRs) against students who participated in peaceful protests over the NEET exam paper leak, even as protest leaders accuse the Centre of reneging on earlier promises to withdraw the cases entirely.

The development marks the latest chapter in a weeks-long standoff between the government and student activists that forced the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan and prompted the biggest street protests of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's third term.

What the Supreme Court Ordered

A bench led by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant, along with Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V. Mohana, passed an interim order on July 28 barring any coercive action against peaceful student protesters. The court directed the immediate release of all minors under 18 detained during the protests who have no criminal history.

The bench also ordered authorities to preserve all surveillance footage — including from drones, body cameras, and CCTV — and barred the publication of protesters' personal data.

"Whoever has committed excess... atrocities on innocent people, the law will take care of them. For that, there needs to be a completely independent and fair investigation."

— Chief Justice Surya Kant, as quoted by Live Law

However, the court refused to stay ongoing investigations into FIRs already registered in connection with the protests, a distinction that has become a flashpoint between the government and protest organizers.

The Government's Assurances and the Trust Deficit

The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), the activist movement spearheading the student agitation, says the Centre's commitment before the Supreme Court falls short of what was promised during direct negotiations. According to CJP spokesperson Saurav Das, the government had assured representatives on July 25, 2026, during talks with Union Ministers J.P. Nadda and Jitendra Singh, that all FIRs against peaceful protesters would be withdrawn and that no student would be targeted for participating in the demonstrations.

Separately, activist Sonam Wangchuk ended a 26-day hunger strike after the government gave a written assurance that cases against students would be taken back if they were not violent, according to The Hindu.

Following the Supreme Court's interim order, however, government officials told CJP leaders the matter was now sub judice, making them unable to provide the promised written assurance regarding FIR withdrawals. Das accused the Centre of "politicising the Supreme Court" by using the judicial proceedings as cover for not honoring its commitments.

Background: From Exam Leaks to Street Protests

The crisis began after question papers for the NEET medical entrance exam, taken by roughly 2 million students in May, were leaked, leading to the exam's cancellation and a re-test on June 21. Protests intensified through July, culminating in a march on Parliament on July 20 that was met with tear gas, baton charges, and — according to media reports verified by The Hindu — pellet guns fired by Rapid Action Force personnel. At least 60 protesters were injured.

One protester, 19-year-old Sahil Lochab, risks losing vision in his right eye after a pellet pierced his pupil. The Central Bureau of Investigation has since filed charges against 13 people connected to the paper leak, including three NTA subject experts and several middlemen, according to Reuters.

Solicitor General Tushar Mehta told the court that while the treatment of students "could not be taken lightly," about 250 police officers were also injured during the clashes.

Diaspora Angle

For Indian students and families abroad, the NEET scandal has reinforced anxieties about the integrity of India's high-stakes examination system — a system that shapes the academic and immigration trajectories of millions, including those who ultimately pursue medical education overseas. Diaspora advocacy groups have closely tracked the government's handling of the protests, particularly allegations of police brutality against young demonstrators.

What's Next

The CJP has warned it will resume nationwide protests if the government does not honor its commitments to withdraw FIRs. The party has demanded that the full details of the July 25 assurances be placed before the Supreme Court during ongoing hearings.

The Delhi High Court is separately hearing petitions on police violence during the July 20 protests and has directed authorities to preserve all relevant footage. That matter returns on September 11.

"A probe is meaningless if no responsibility is fixed."

— Chief Justice Surya Kant

Meanwhile, the Modi government has introduced a bill in Parliament to amend public examination legislation, proposing prison terms of five to 10 years and fines up to 50 million rupees ($522,000) for those involved in exam fraud — a legislative response that may outlast the political crisis but does little to resolve the fate of hundreds of students still facing criminal cases for taking to the streets.
